dialogue.literal_gloss: Kwedu [kwedu] • kune [to / at ne] • makomo [mountains] • marefu [plural refu] • anonakidza [he/she nakidza] • kuona [to / at ona]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anonakidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anonakidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('Kwedu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'Kwedu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

grammar_notes.title: Expressing 'Has/Have' and 'There Is/Are' ('-ne' & 'pane / kune')
grammar_notes.content: Shona does not use a separate verb like 'have'; instead, it combines a subject prefix with '-ne' ('with'). For people: 'ndine' (I have), 'une' (you have), 'ane' (he/she has), 'tine' (we have), 'vane' (they have). For things, the prefix matches the object: 'imba ine...' ('the house has...'), 'rori rine...' ('the truck has...'). When combined with the location prefixes 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-', it means 'there is / there are': 'pane' ('there is right here'), 'kune' ('there is in that area'), and 'mune' ('there is inside').
grammar_notes.rule: Person/Thing + -ne = has/have (tine = we have, ine = it has) | pane / kune / mune = there is / there are

cultural_notes.title: Zimbabwe's Dramatic Mountain Landscapes ('Makomo Marefu')
cultural_notes.content: From the mist-covered peaks of the Eastern Highlands—Mount Nyangani (2,592m), the Chimanimani Mountains, and the Bvumba—to the ancient granite inselbergs ('makomo') and balancing rocks of Matobo, Domboshava, and Epworth, mountain landscapes hold deep scenic and historical significance across Zimbabwe.

dialogue.literal_gloss: Ugosvika [ugosvika] • pano [right here (at this spot)] • manhero [in the evening] • kuti [that / so that] • tigozodya [tigozodya] • tese [tese]

grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('manhero')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'manhero'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Pointing Out Things: Demonstratives ('pano' = 'this / that / here')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, words for 'this/these' and 'that/those' (like 'pano') come AFTER the noun they point to and mirror the noun's group! Near demonstratives ('this / these / right here') repeat the noun class vowel: 'mwana uyu' (this child), 'nyama iyi' (this meat), 'kapu iyi' (this cup), 'bhuku iri' (this book), 'zvinhu izvi' (these things). Replacing the final vowel with '-o' shifts the meaning to 'that / those / there': 'uyo' (that person), 'iyo' (that one), 'uko' (over there).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Near Demonstrative ('uyu/iyi/iri/ichi/izvi' = this/these) | replace final vowel with '-o' ('uyo/iyo/iro/icho/izvo' = that/those)

cultural_notes.title: Evening Hospitality & Saving a Plate ('Kuchengetera Munhu Chikafu')
cultural_notes.content: Communal eating ('kudya tese' — eating together) cements family bonds in Shona culture. Even if a relative is delayed until late evening ('manhero'), the cook always sets aside a generous covered portion near the hearth so no member of the home ever goes hungry.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakanyanya')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakanyanya' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('kunze')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'kunze'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Summer Thunderstorms ('Mvura Iri Kunaya Zvakanyanya') on the Plateau
cultural_notes.content: During the peak rainy months of December, January ('Ndira'), and February ('Kukadzi'), intense afternoon downpours sweep across the Zimbabwean plateau. While heavy rain ('mvura iri kunaya zvakanyanya') keeps people indoors for an hour or two, it is celebrated as a blessing ('makomborero') that fills rivers and nourishes the maize crop.

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('ravo')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'ravo' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'neuto'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'neuto'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'uto' forms 'neuto'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('hwaizivikanwa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'hwaizivikanwa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

cultural_notes.title: The Rozvi Empire ('Humambo hweRozvi') & Changamire Dombo
cultural_notes.content: Founded in the late 17th century by the military strategist Changamire Dombo, the Rozvi Empire ('Humambo hweRozvi') ruled much of the Zimbabwean plateau until the 1830s. Renowned for its disciplined army ('uto') that expelled Portuguese forces in the 1690s, the Rozvi built magnificent patterned dry-stone capitals at Danangombe (Dhlo-Dhlo) and Naletale.

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'nevatorwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'nevatorwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. cultural_notes.title: Pre-Colonial Gold ('Ndarama') & Ivory ('Nyanga dzeNzou') Trade Routes
cultural_notes.content: For over a millennium before colonial rule, Shona kingdoms—including Mapungubwe, Great Zimbabwe, Mutapa, and Torwa—conducted thriving international commerce. Gold ('ndarama') panned from rivers and mined from quartz reefs, along with elephant ivory ('nyanga dzenzou'), was traded along the Save and Zambezi valleys to Indian Ocean merchants ('vatorwa') from Kilwa, Sofala, Arabia, and Asia.

For example, 'ne-' + 'tsika' forms 'netsika'. grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Nhoroondo dzekare dzinotidzidzisa kwatakabva netsika dzedu semaShona.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: Oral History ('Nhoroondo'), Totems ('Mitupo') & Shona Identity
cultural_notes.content: Knowledge of family and national history ('nhoroondo dzekare') is passed down through clan praise poetry ('nhetembo dzorudzi') and totems ('mitupo'—such as 'Mhofu' Eland, 'Shumba' Lion, 'Soko' Vervet Monkey, 'Nzou' Elephant, and 'Gumbo' Leg). Knowing one's history and totem teaches kinship ties, marriage exogamy rules, and shared cultural values ('tsika dzedu semaShona').

sections.heading: 2. Core Shona Grammar Rules Consolidated
points: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anonakidza'): [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)
Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('manhero'): Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Zimbabwe's Dramatic Mountain Landscapes ('Makomo Marefu'): From the mist-covered peaks of the Eastern Highlands—Mount Nyangani (2,592m), the Chimanimani Mountains, and the Bvumba—to the ancient granite inselbergs ('makomo') and balancing rocks of Matobo, Domboshava, and Epworth, mountain landscapes hold deep scenic and historical significance across Zimbabwe..
Evening Hospitality & Saving a Plate ('Kuchengetera Munhu Chikafu'): Communal eating ('kudya tese' — eating together) cements family bonds in Shona culture.

Summer Thunderstorms ('Mvura Iri Kunaya Zvakanyanya') on the Plateau: During the peak rainy months of December, January ('Ndira'), and February ('Kukadzi'), intense afternoon downpours sweep across the Zimbabwean plateau.

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nembariro'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nembariro'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'mbariro' forms 'nembariro'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('yaivakwa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'yaivakwa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'yaivakwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'yaivakwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.
grammar_notes.rule: Verb Root + -wa / -iwa = Passive ('be [verb]-ed') -> -bika (cook) -> -bikwa (be cooked); -vaka (build) -> -vakwa (be built)

cultural_notes.title: Traditional Shona Architecture: Pole, Dagga & Thatch ('Mbariro neHuswa')
cultural_notes.content: Traditional rural homesteads ('misha yechinyakare') feature round kitchens ('imba yekubikira') and sleeping huts built with earthen brick or clay walls, roofed with a conical framework of sturdy wooden poles ('mbariro') tied with bark fibre ('rwodzi') and expertly thatched with bundled savannah grass ('huswa'). Unlike corrugated iron sheets ('marata'), grass thatch keeps the room naturally cool in summer and warm in winter.

dialogue.literal_gloss: Wakamboenda [you/he (past) mboenda] • kunzvimbo [to / at nzvimbo] • dzinochengetedza [dzinochengetedza] • nhoroondo [nhoroondo] • dzenyika [dzenyika] • yedu [yedu] • yekare [yekare] • here [(yes/no question marker)]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('Wakamboenda')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Wakamboenda' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('yedu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'yedu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

cultural_notes.title: Zimbabwe's UNESCO Heritage Sites & Historical Monuments
cultural_notes.content: Zimbabwe preserves extraordinary ancient heritage sites ('nzvimbo dzinochengetedza nhoroondo') across the country: Great Zimbabwe in Masvingo, the terraced stone platforms of Khami near Bulawayo, the ancient agricultural stone terraces and pit structures ('matanga') of Ziwa in Nyanga, and thousands of San and Shona rock art sites in the Matobo Hills.

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anoti')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anoti' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('mavara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'mavara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('matatu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'matatu' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

cultural_notes.title: Flag Colours, Design & the National Symbols of Zimbabwe
cultural_notes.content: Adopted at Independence on 18 April 1980, Zimbabwe's national flag ('mureza weZimbabwe') is rich in symbolism: green represents agriculture and the land's flora, yellow stands for mineral wealth (gold, platinum, and diamonds), red commemorates the blood shed for independence, black represents the heritage of the majority population, white symbolizes peace, and the soapstone Zimbabwe Bird ('Hungwe') connects the modern nation to Great Zimbabwe.

cultural_notes.title: Tropical Fruit Growing ('Chinanasi') in Zimbabwe's Eastern Highlands
cultural_notes.content: Thanks to high rainfall, fertile red soils, and warm valleys in Manicaland's Rusitu Valley, Chipinge, and Honde Valley, Zimbabwe grows sweet tropical fruits ('michero') including pineapples ('zvinanasi'), bananas, avocados, macadamia nuts, and tea on lush mountain slopes.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('wakapamhamha')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'wakapamhamha' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'unoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Zimbabwe's Trunk Highways & Seasonal Savannah Grass ('Sora Rakaoma')
cultural_notes.content: Major tarred highways ('migwagwa ine tara') link Harare with Bulawayo, Mutare, Masvingo, and Chirundu across the high savannah plateau. During the dry winter and spring months from June to October, the roadside savannah grass ('sora') turns golden and dry ('rakaoma') beneath deep-rooted indigenous trees that stay green all year round.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakatakura')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakatakura' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('chena')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'chena'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Urban Commuter Minibuses ('Makombi') & Suburban Transit

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Traditional Shona Architecture: Pole, Dagga & Thatch ('Mbariro neHuswa'): Traditional rural homesteads ('misha yechinyakare') feature round kitchens ('imba yekubikira') and sleeping huts built with earthen brick or clay walls, roofed with a conical framework of sturdy wooden poles ('mbariro') tied with bark fibre ('rwodzi') and expertly thatched with bundled savannah grass ('huswa').

Zimbabwe's UNESCO Heritage Sites & Historical Monuments: Zimbabwe preserves extraordinary ancient heritage sites ('nzvimbo dzinochengetedza nhoroondo') across the country: Great Zimbabwe in Masvingo, the terraced stone platforms of Khami near Bulawayo, the ancient agricultural stone terraces and pit structures ('matanga') of Ziwa in Nyanga, and thousands of San and Shona rock art sites in the Matobo Hills..

Flag Colours, Design & the National Symbols of Zimbabwe: Adopted at Independence on 18 April 1980, Zimbabwe's national flag ('mureza weZimbabwe') is rich in symbolism: green represents agriculture and the land's flora, yellow stands for mineral wealth (gold, platinum, and diamonds), red commemorates the blood shed for independence, black represents the heritage of the majority population, white symbolizes peace, and the soapstone Zimbabwe Bird ('Hungwe') connects the modern nation to Great Zimbabwe..

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('dzakaunganidzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'dzakaunganidzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('dzitema')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'dzitema'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Open-Air Clothing Markets ('Mabhero' / 'Kotamai') & Local Fashion
cultural_notes.content: Across Zimbabwean towns and growth points, open-air clothing markets are popular places to shop for affordable, stylish garments ('mbatya' or 'hembe') and hats ('ngowani'). Because shoppers often bend down to inspect neatly stacked piles of clothing on clean groundsheets, such markets are affectionately nicknamed 'kotamai' ('bend down and choose!').

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('mitatu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'mitatu' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

cultural_notes.title: The Sitting Room ('Imba Yokutandarira') & Zimbabwean Wood & Stone Carvings
cultural_notes.content: Literally meaning 'the room for relaxing and conversing together', the 'imba yokutandarira' is the pride of a Zimbabwean home. Alongside upholstered sofas ('zvigaro zvomutefetefe') and cushions ('mitsago'), many families decorate their coffee tables with hand-carved wooden or serpentine stone sculptures ('zvivezwa') crafted by local Zimbabwean artists.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Parutivi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Parutivi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Homestead Garden Tools ('Maturusi') & Local Blacksmith Craftsmanship
cultural_notes.content: Every rural and suburban household in Zimbabwe keeps a set of sturdy hand tools—hoes ('mabadza'), rakes ('mahara'), digging forks ('mafoko'), and shovels ('mafoshoro')—fitted with carved hardwood handles ('mibato yemuti') to prepare vegetable beds and clear stony yard paths.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakachenuruka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakachenuruka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('ruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'ruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('mbiri')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'mbiri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('dzakawanda')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'dzakawanda' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('zvinosanganisira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvinosanganisira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: Springtime 'Kupfumvutira' of Indigenous Trees & School Stationery Shops
cultural_notes.content: Notice the expressive verb 'kupfumvutira'—the bursting forth of fresh new leaves on roadside trees in spring (September–October), when Zimbabwe's 'musasa' trees flush in brilliant shades of bronze, crimson, and fresh green before the rains! Meanwhile, town shops ('zvitoro') stock up on books ('mabhuku'), pens ('zvinyoreso'), and glue for the school term.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

Shoppers carry their purchases home in colourful woven checkered carrier bags colloquially known across Southern Africa as 'mashangani' bags.

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Open-Air Clothing Markets ('Mabhero' / 'Kotamai') & Local Fashion: Across Zimbabwean towns and growth points, open-air clothing markets are popular places to shop for affordable, stylish garments ('mbatya' or 'hembe') and hats ('ngowani').

The Sitting Room ('Imba Yokutandarira') & Zimbabwean Wood & Stone Carvings: Literally meaning 'the room for relaxing and conversing together', the 'imba yokutandarira' is the pride of a Zimbabwean home.

Cold Drinks ('Zvinwiwa'), Mazoe Orange Crush & Afternoon Hospitality: On warm afternoons in Zimbabwe, welcoming a guest to the table with a cold glass of cordial—most famously Zimbabwe's iconic Mazoe Orange Crush diluted with chilled water and ice cubes ('magodo echando' from the 'firiji')—or a bottled soft drink ('chigubhu chedhiringi') is a beloved tradition of home hospitality..

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 57: Shangu yakagadzikwa parutivi rwematayera ndeye bhurauni...
lessons.shona_text: Shangu yakagadzikwa parutivi rwematayera ndeye bhurauni mukati mayowo muri bhurauni ine kasimbi pamusoro kumberi kwayo kwakatesvera uye kunovhara zvigunwe zvese kana yakapfekwa. Vanhu vazhinji vane mizera yakasiyana vanosanganisira varume nevakadzi varikuita zvakasiyana vamwe vakamira vamwe vari kufamba vamwe ndivo vari kuratidza kuti vari kutengesa zvinhu zvakasiyana.
lessons.english_translation: A brown shoe is placed beside the tiles; its interior is also brown and it has a small metal buckle on top, with a pointed toe that covers all the toes when worn. Nearby, many people of different ages—both men and women—are engaged in various activities: some standing, some walking, and others selling assorted goods.

dialogue.shona: Shangu yakagadzikwa parutivi rwematayera ndeye bhurauni mukati mayowo muri bhurauni ine kasimbi pamusoro kumberi kwayo kwakatesvera uye kunovhara zvigunwe zvese kana yakapfekwa.
dialogue.english: A shoe placed beside the tiles is brown inside and out, with a small metal clasp on top and a pointed front that covers the toes when worn.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakagadzikwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakagadzikwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('kunovhara')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'kunovhara' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 58: Musha wakapakwa mota yerudzi rutema, pane...
lessons.shona_text: Musha wakapakwa mota yerudzi rutema, pane muti wemupichisi une mashizha akasvibira uyewo pamusoro pejurahoro panoonekwa zvidhinha zvakarongwa zvakawandira mukati Motikari yakamira pamumugwagwa inozivikanwa ichinzi gonyeti.Ine musoro muhombe ine ruvara rutsvuku nesirivha.Pamhiri pari kuonekwa imba yakavakwa ichiita kunge mahofisi ine midhuri yeruvara rweorenji nezvichena nemiti iri kureba iri kumera ipapo.
lessons.english_translation: At a homestead, a black car is parked near a peach tree with green leaves, and on top of the wall many neatly stacked bricks can be seen. A large haulage truck (gonyeti) with a red and silver cab is parked by the road. Across the way stands an office-like building with orange and white walls surrounded by tall growing trees.

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 59: Munhukadzi ari kugadzirwa musoro wake. Uso...
lessons.shona_text: Munhukadzi ari kugadzirwa musoro wake. Uso hwake hausi kuonekwa asi pane ruoko rwuri mumusoro runoita senge ndiro ruri kugadzira bvudzi. Ari kumonwa tumabhanzi turi kuinda tuchidonhera kusvika nechekuda kuenzana namapendekete. Bvudzi idema pasi asi pamusoro rakatsvukuruka. Rakapfava zvinoratidza kuti rakaiswa mushonga. Vanhu vaviri vomutambo wonhabvu. Vakapfeka mayunifomu akafanana. Umwe chete akaisa chichena pamusoro. Vanoratidza kuti varipakudzidzira mutambo wawo uye vose vari kukwikwidzana kuti vagone kukava bhora riri nechepasi.
lessons.english_translation: A woman is having her hair styled. Her face is not visible, but a stylist's hand can be seen braiding her hair into neat twists that fall toward her shoulders. The hair is black at the roots and reddish-brown toward the tips, looking soft and treated. In another scene, two football players in matching uniforms—one wearing a white cap—are training and competing to kick the ball on the ground.

dialogue.shona: Munhukadzi ari kugadzirwa musoro wake. Uso hwake hausi kuonekwa asi pane ruoko rwuri mumusoro runoita senge ndiro ruri kugadzira bvudzi.
dialogue.english: A woman is having her hair styled; her face is not visible, but a hand can be seen working on her hair.

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 60: Pakati pevanhu vari kufamba muguta parutivi...
lessons.shona_text: Pakati pevanhu vari kufamba muguta parutivi rwemugwagwae pane murume akapfeka hembe yeruvara rutsvuku nomudhebhe weruvara ruchena pamwe chete neshangu dziri muruvara rutema. Matakishopu maviri. Imwe yakapendwa nependi chena imwe yakapendwa nependi yegirinhi uye pamusoro yakanyorwa. Zvekare matakishopu aya ari pedo nematombo. Midziyo yomumba kana kuti makabati maviri arimuchitoro arikutengeswa. Makabati acho akapendwa nependi chena, uye akaiswa mapatani mapatani mberi, kuitira kunakisa mumba maanenge aiswa.

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('yeruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'yeruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('vakaungana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vakaungana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('zvinove')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvinove' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('rima')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'rima' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Footwear Craftsmanship ('Shangu') & Bustling Town Walkways: Zimbabwe has a long tradition of leatherwork and footwear manufacturing (centered historically in Gweru with companies like Bata), alongside skilled roadside cobblers who keep leather shoes ('shangu') polished and repaired for busy city life..

Backyard Peach Trees ('Mupichisi'), Brick Stacking & Haulage 'Magonyeti': This vivid passage captures three everyday sights in Zimbabwean peri-urban neighbourhoods: a fruiting peach tree ('muti wemupichisi') in the yard, stacks of clay bricks ('zvidhinha') ready for home extensions, and a massive intercity haulage truck—universally called a 'gonyeti'—parked along the main road..

Hair Braiding ('Kuruka Bvudzi') & Zimbabwe's Passion for Football ('Nhabvu'): This two-part passage highlights two pillars of contemporary Zimbabwean culture: intricate hairstyling ('kugadzirwa musoro' and twisting braids 'tumabhanzi'), which is both an art form and a social occasion, and football ('nhabvu' or 'bhora')—the country's most popular sport, played passionately in every neighbourhood and stadium..

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('wakadzima')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'wakadzima' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unoshandiswa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'unoshandiswa' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: City Traffic Lights ('Marobhotsi') & Stadium Football Culture ('Munhandare')
cultural_notes.content: Notice two classic Zimbabwean terms in this passage: 'marobhotsi' (traffic lights, painted with black-and-white striped poles at city intersections to prevent collisions) and 'nhandare' (a sports stadium), where thousands of supporters ('vaokeri') gather on weekends to cheer their favourite football clubs!

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 65: Rori huru kwazvo rakamira zvaro. Rori...
lessons.shona_text: Rori huru kwazvo rakamira zvaro. Rori iri rine musoro muchena uye rakanaka zvikuru pakutarisa. Rinoratidza kuti rinogona kutakura zvinhu zvakawanda kwazvo uye rori iri riri panzvimbo inoratidza kuti inzvimbo yekuwedzera mafuta. Shangu dzekurudyi nedzekuruboshwe. Dzine ruvara rwebhuruu neruchena. Dzinoratidza kuti dzakambopfekwa nekuti dzaakukwatanuka. Dzine tambo chena. Shangu idzi dzinogona kupfekwa zvose nevanhurume kana vanhukadzi. Vanhu vakamira padivi pemotokari dzemarudzi rwemakombi mukati meguta nechekumberi kune imba hombe yemudurikanidzwa yakabaka magetsi mukati mayo. Masvingo eGreat Zimbabwe izvi zvinova zvivakwa zvematombo zviri munzvimbo yeMasvingo. Inzvimbo inonyanyawo kushanyirwa nevanhu vachiona mararamiro aiitawo vanhu kare uyewo pane vanhu vari kuratidza kuti vakamira vauya kuzoshanya panzvimbo iyi.
lessons.english_translation: A huge truck is parked; it has a handsome white cab, can carry heavy loads, and is stopped at a fuel station. Nearby are left and right blue-and-white shoes with white laces that can be worn by men or women. In the city, people stand beside commuter minibuses (makombi) with a lit multi-storey building ahead. Finally, the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe in Masvingo are shown—a famous heritage site visited by many people to see how ancestors lived long ago.
